newsitem.title: UK: Legal experts say euro transition not watertight.
newsitem.headline: Legal experts say euro transition not watertight.

text.p: A European single currency would be sheltered by a broad legal framework but some loopholes may still threaten the continuity of existing contracts, legal experts said on Friday.
A London conference was told that problems could arise in terms of contractual obligations, particularly concerning bond and loan agreements, between the United States and countries in the euro zone.

"In general corporate terms it's not a disaster, continuity is at least broadly preserved," said Jeremy Thomas, partner at solicitors Allen & Overy, addressing a conference here on the Legal Implications of a Single Currency.
But he added that the current legal framework had left some residual litigation risk. Specifically, rules for avoiding force majeure were not watertight.
The Maastrich Treaty states that the introduction of the euro, planned for January 1, 1999, will not lead to any unilateral termination of legal contracts or alteration of any of the terms.
Legal experts said existing contracts were mostly safe.

"Disappearance should not entitle a party to terminate the contract, unless parties have agreed that this should be the outcome," said Iona Levine, head of derivatives at UK-based solicitors Hammond Suddards.
But she added that Ecu-based agreements could be vulnerable as some countries might not recognise the euro as a successor to Ecu which is made up of a basket of currencies.
Defaults on the basis of the doctrine of frustration was unlikely. This enables a party to unilaterally treat their obligations as terminated as a result of a supervening event.
But in cases involving a swap agreement between two euro-zone currencies, parties could argue that the need for currency hedging has been eliminated, thus rendering the contract invalid.
Corine Bouffandeau, head of the French practice of Hammond Suddards, said under French law neither force majeure nor the frustration argument was fulfilled.
But countries with a common law legal system, such as the United States, had expressed concerns about the legal complications involving the transition to the euro.
"There would be ground for litigation on the basis of impossibility of performance or frustration of purpose," she said

Michael Gruson, partner at U.S.-based solicitors Shearman & Sterling, however said there was no room for non-performance because non-introduction of the euro could not have been a basic assumption of a contractual agreement drawn after the Maastrich Treaty.
In any event, New York's legislative assembly was considering the adoption of a statutory amendment to the General Obligations Bill to deal with continuity of contracts.
